title: Sexual conduct
hookLine: precept three: refrain from sexual misconduct; harm, not shame, is the measure

cards: Of the five precepts, this is the one a listener might brace for: a list of forbidden things, a raised eyebrow, the feeling of being judged before a word is said.
But the way teachers explain it today, shame isn't its measure. It asks the same question the first two precepts asked about life and about things: is anyone being harmed?

teach.b: In Pali: Kamesu micchacara veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. I undertake the training rule to refrain from misconduct in sensual pleasures. Kama means sensual pleasure, desire.
Micchacara means wrong conduct, literally going the wrong way.
The precept doesn't name desire itself. Lay Buddhists marry, fall in love, raise families, and the texts treat that as a normal human life. It names going the wrong way with desire.
The early discourses make that concrete: someone who keeps this precept doesn't get involved with people who are under someone else's protection, or promised to someone else.
In the world those texts came from, that meant a daughter in her family's care, or a wife or a betrothed woman.

teach.h: THE OLD LIST IS ABOUT HARM.
teach.b: Teachers today read one thread through that list: harm, to the other person, to a partner who trusted you, to families. So they often put it in a single line: harm, not shame, is the measure.
Honesty, consent, keeping the promises you've made, not using another person. Buddhist communities read the details in different ways, and it's fair to say so plainly.
More traditional communities keep closely to the old lists.
Other teachers, especially in newer communities, focus on the principle of not causing harm and apply it to every kind of relationship. Monks and nuns go further still: they keep complete celibacy.
What they all share is the heart of it. Desire is human. What you do with it can heal or wound.
The precept is a training in the first.

how: Lay Buddhists recite the third precept with the other four; communities interpret its details differently, and monks and nuns keep full celibacy under their monastic rule.

o: loving in ways that harm no one
giving up love and family life

games.q: match the piece of the third precept.
p: wrong conduct; going the wrong way

s: the third precept teaches that desire itself is shameful
it names going the wrong way with desire; lay Buddhists marry and raise families.
the old texts describe the precept with a list of people under someone else's protection
teachers read harm as the thread through that list: to the other person and to those who trusted them.
all Buddhist communities read the details of this precept the same way
traditional communities keep closely to the old lists; many teachers apply the principle of not harming to every relationship.

games.q: a friend asks what the third precept actually measures. what do you tell them?
games.why: harm is the thread: to the other person, to a partner who trusted you, to families. that's why teachers say harm, not shame, is the measure.

practice: Bring to mind someone close to you, a partner, a friend, a parent, a child, and one promise you've made them, big or small: I'll be home by six, I'll call you back, I'll be honest with you.

Hold that promise gently, like something that belongs to both of you, and notice the trust inside it. Then, if you like, send them the old wish from the metta weeks: may you be safe, may you be at ease.

wordCard.voice: Sexual conduct. The third precept: a training not to go the wrong way with desire, where the measure is harm, not shame.

orig.note: Pali: wrong conduct, literally 'going the wrong way'; in the precept, wrong conduct in sensual pleasures (kamesu).

carryVoice: Your line: no harm in love. Harm, not shame, is the measure. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 41 (Saleyyaka Sutta), the list of those under protection
